metadata.title: Logistic regression: a linear score, a probability, a boundary
metadata.subject: AI/ML
metadata.objective: Show a decision boundary and how predicted probability changes with a feature.
misconceptions: Logistic regression predicts a class directly with a straight line
The boundary is the same thing as the probability curve
expectedUnderstanding: The linear score s = w·x + b is the input; the sigmoid turns it into a probability strictly between 0 and 1.
At s = 0 the probability is 0.5, so the decision boundary is the score-0 line; on this one-feature plot that is the vertical line x = 0.
Moving the feature moves the point along the fixed logistic curve; the class label is produced only afterwards by a 0.5 threshold rule.
The curve approaches 0 and 1 but never reaches or passes them, so a predicted probability cannot exceed 1.

primitives.text: Score s = w·x + b, here w = 1 and b = 0. Probability p = 1/(1+e^-s), always between 0 and 1.
The boundary is s = 0, so p = 0.5: predict class 1 above the line, class 0 below.
Logistic regression: a linear score, a probability, a boundary

checkpoints.title: Left of the boundary
checkpoints.body: Pick a feature value to the left of the dashed boundary. Is the predicted probability above or below 0.5? Move the slider to check.

checkpoints.title: Crossing x = 0
checkpoints.body: Move the feature across the boundary. What changes at that exact point: the score, the predicted probability, or the class decision?

checkpoints.title: Close to one
checkpoints.body: At x = 3 the bar is close to the top. Why can the predicted probability never reach or exceed 1?

checkpoints.title: Class or probability
checkpoints.body: Does the model output the class directly, or does it output a probability that a separate 0.5 rule turns into a class?

narration.text: Blue points are class 0 and red points are class 1. The curve is the predicted probability that the label is 1, not the label itself.
The score s = w·x + b is linear. The sigmoid maps that score to a probability between 0 and 1, so a larger score never means a probability above 1.
At s = 0 the probability is exactly 0.5. That score is the decision boundary; on this plot it is the red dashed line at x = 0, where the prediction flips.
Far to the right the curve approaches 1 from below, and far to the left it approaches 0 from above. The threshold at 0.5 turns the probability into a class after the fact.

fallback.text: Static plot of predicted probability against one feature. The horizontal axis runs from about minus 4 to 4 and the vertical axis from 0 to 1, with a dashed line at 0.5 and a red dashed vertical boundary at x = 0. The black S-curve is p = 1/(1+e^-x). Blue points at p = 0 sit at x = -3.1 and -1.8; red points at p = 1 sit at x = 1.8 and 3.1. A blue bar at x = 0.6 rises to about 0.65, showing the current prediction. As x moves from -2.6 through 0 to 2.6 the bar rises from about 0.07 through 0.5 to about 0.93, while the curve never crosses 0 or 1. Caption: the linear score is the input; the sigmoid gives a probability; the 0.5 threshold gives the class; the boundary is at score 0.
